text:
The season that comes after autumn is winter.

The air in the Grand Culinary Arena was thick with the scent of vanilla and panic. Contestant Gary, a man whose confidence was directly proportional to the amount of butter in his recipe, froze. His eyes darted from the bowl of granulated sugar to the identical-looking bowl of coarse sea salt. In a moment of sheer, unadulterated brain-fart, he reached for the salt.

He poured it into his chocolate fudge cake batter. He baked it. He frosted it. He presented it to the judges, a panel of three stern food critics who looked like they hadn’t smiled since the invention of the microwave.

Gary stared at his cake. It was perfect. It was also going to taste like a beach exploded inside a chocolate factory. He looked at the judges. He looked at his competitors, who were currently piping delicate rosettes of buttercream. Gary’s mind raced. He couldn’t lose. Not here. Not now.

"Ladies and gentlemen," Gary announced, his voice cracking only slightly. "What you are about to taste is not a mistake. It is a revolution. I call it... The Umami Dilemma."

The head judge, a woman named Madame Vane who wore sunglasses indoors, raised an eyebrow. "Umami?"

"Savory notes to cut the cloying sweetness of modern dessert culture," Gary lied, sweating profusely. "It’s a trend. A bold, new trend. And I’m not the only one brave enough to try it."

He turned to the baker next to him, a sweet-faced woman named Linda who was making a lemon tart. "Linda! You’re doing a lemon tart? Why not add a pinch of smoked paprika? Or maybe some miso? It’s called 'Gourmet Contrast.' Everyone’s doing it."

Linda blinked. "Everyone is?"

"Everyone," Gary said, pointing aggressively at the guy making a cheesecake. "Hey, Steve! Your cheesecake needs a kick! Add some soy sauce! It’s the future!"

Steve, confused but desperate to not be left behind, nodded and began drizzling soy sauce over his cream cheese mixture. Within minutes, the competition had devolved into a chaotic experiment in culinary heresy.
